Cutting Grass, Cutting Pollution: Where Electric Lawn Equipment Matters Most

By Sav Maive | Updated: October 19, 2026
Studies
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 11:04
Instaread

As fall cleanup ramps up, Baltimore and Alexandria, Virginia, are moving to ban gas-powered leaf blowers, and New York is creating a statewide rebate program for electric lawn care equipment. But in Florida, a new state law overrides local bans.

With loud leaf blowers revving up across the U.S., LawnStarter looked at over 650 U.S. counties to map Where Electric Lawn Equipment Matters Most.

We ranked counties based on how much pollution their lawn equipment produces, how much lawn and green space there is to maintain, and how much air pollution residents already face, factors that together indicate where switching to electric equipment could have the greatest potential benefit.

See how your county’s air quality could be impacted below, with insights from fully electric lawn care crews, clean air advocates, and local government leaders. To learn more about the data we used, check out our methodology.

Relevant Terms: Pollutants from Gas-Powered Lawn Equipment

Key Definitions

  • Small Off-Road Engines (SORE) | Spark-ignition engines rated at 19 kilowatts or below that are commonly used in lawn care and gardening. In California, smog-forming emissions from SORE are projected to be nearly 2X those of light-duty passenger cars by 2031.
  • 2-Stroke Engines | The type of engine commonly found in leaf blowers, string trimmers, and chainsaws. These accounted for an estimated 82% of PM 2.5 emissions from lawn equipment nationwide in 2020.
  • 4-Stroke Engines | The type of engine commonly found in lawn mowers and garden tractors. They are more fuel-efficient than 2-stroke engines because lubricating oil is kept separately from the fuel, while in 2-stroke engines, oil and fuel are mixed and expelled in the exhaust. 
  • PM 2.5 | PM means particulate matter, which is a combination of solid pollution particles and liquid in the air. PM 2.5 are fine particles with a diameter of 2.5 micrometers or smaller. Exposure can increase the risk of heart disease, stroke, and lung cancer. 
  • CO2 | Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas, produced when gasoline is burned to power gas-powered equipment. 
  • NOx | Nitrogen oxides (a combination of nitric oxide and nitrogen dioxide) can form lung-damaging ground-level ozone and also contribute to acid rain. 
  • VOC | Volatile organic compounds come from unburned fuel in equipment exhaust and from fuel evaporating during use and refilling.
  • CO | Carbon monoxide is a toxic, colorless, and odorless gas emitted from gas-powered equipment that can cause headaches, fatigue, dizziness, and cardiovascular stress.
  • O3 | Ground-level ozone is a gas that’s formed when NOx and VOCs react, typically spiking on hot summer days. This colorless gas can cause respiratory issues and can also impact plant growth.

5 Counties Where Going Electric Could Have the Biggest Impact

Our top 5 counties cover just 2% of the land area we analyzed, but account for nearly 9% of the lawn-equipment VOC emissions in this report. Across the 5 counties, CO2 emissions from lawn equipment in 2020 were equivalent to roughly 370,000 passenger vehicles’ annual emissions.

Counties are shown in rank order, 1 to 5.

Harris County, TXNo. 1

Biggest cities: Houston, Pasadena, Baytown

85,000 carsAnnual emissions equivalent of this county's 2020 lawn-equipment CO2

CO2 emissions from lawn equipment in Harris County in 2020 were equivalent to emissions from 85,000 cars. Harris County has the 11th worst Median Air Quality Index out of the counties in our ranking, with 38 days of unhealthy air quality in 2025.

Texas (alongside Florida and Georgia) has a preemption law, prohibiting counties, municipalities, and districts from banning the use of gas-powered lawn equipment.

Harris County Universal Services was recognized in NAFA’s Green Garage contest at the beginning of this year, highlighting sustainable initiatives across county Fleet Services operations, including Precinct 2 adopting battery-powered equipment and park fleets going fully electric.

Lawn Pro Perspectives: Benefits of Electric Equipment

Upgrading equipment can be a big investment, especially for lawn care pros whose commercial mowing equipment costs significantly more than residential lawn mowers.

But beyond saving the environment, electric equipment can help crews save money on fuel and also avoid the health impacts from noise pollution and spending hours inhaling exhaust fumes.

We turned to Kevin Boodram of Serenity Robotic Lawncare and to Oscar Ortega and JT Wilkinson, maintenance care managers for FormLA Landscaping, Inc., to learn more about their experiences switching to electric. Read their insights below.

Note: While both companies below utilized local incentives for purchasing electric equipment, it’s important to keep in mind that not all rebate programs are alike. Some have requirements, like turning in a working gas-powered device. Some are more substantial than others.

  1. What sparked the switch to electric lawn care equipment?
  2. Did you participate in any local rebate programs when upgrading your equipment? If so, what was that experience like?
  3. How has working without direct gas exhaust and fuel fumes affected the daily physical health and energy levels of your crew?
  4. Do your clients notice a difference in your equipment choices?
  5. What operational realities (battery rotation, charging logistics) should other contractors know if they want to reduce their fleet’s environmental footprint?
  6. Did savings on fuel and oil costs offset the upfront cost of commercial battery banks as quickly as projected?
Kevin Boodram
CEO
Serenity Robotic Lawncare, Huntington, New York

What sparked the switch to electric lawn care equipment?

Noise was the biggest motivation. I was in school during the pandemic, and gas leaf blowers kept waking me up and interrupting my remote classes. It was frustrating, and I noticed other people felt the same way — some were volunteering their time to advocate for restrictions on gas equipment.

My thinking was that if people cared enough to organize around this issue, there must be a market for a quieter service. I wanted to offer a market-based solution: Give homeowners a landscaping company they could choose that respected their peace and quiet.

Did you participate in any local rebate programs when upgrading your equipment?

We used some rebates offered by our local utility, PSEG Long Island, for equipment purchases early on. That was several years ago, so I don’t recall the exact amounts or program details.

The more significant support came from over $23,000 in private grants through business competitions. Our focus on innovation and environmentally friendly equipment helped us make a compelling case. We also bought some used equipment when starting out, which stretched that funding considerably and covered much of our initial equipment investment.

How has working without direct gas exhaust and fuel fumes affected the daily physical health and energy levels of your crew?

In my experience, electric equipment makes the workday much less physically taxing. We occasionally still rent gas aerators, although we’re moving toward equipment we can pull with our electric mowers. Going back to gas equipment really makes the noise and vibration stand out. Personally, I find that exhausting after a few hours.

Beyond avoiding exhaust and fuel fumes, reliability makes a big difference in how the day feels. With gas equipment, a difficult start can interrupt the whole workflow. With our electric equipment, we can get to a property, pick up a tool, and get to work. That smoother rhythm reduces frustration and helps us maintain our energy. These are observations from our daily experience rather than measured health outcomes.

Do your clients notice a difference in your equipment choices?

Absolutely. Some clients have even offered to pay more than our asking price because they wanted to support quieter equipment and help our business grow. They see hiring us as a way to encourage change in the industry.

One customer described us as “ninjas”: they would go into a meeting with an overgrown lawn, come out to find it cut, and never realize we had been there. That captures what customers appreciate—the lawn gets maintained without disrupting their day.

What operational realities should other contractors know?

Electric equipment requires planning and retraining, especially for people accustomed to gas equipment. In our operation, it can take roughly a month for an experienced gas-equipment operator to get comfortable with our summer workflow.

Efficiency matters. I spend time watching the crew work and looking for unnecessary steps, repeated passes, or situations where one person blows debris back into an area someone else has already cleared. We plan battery rotation and charging around the day’s workload and keep extra batteries available.

I think of this as conserving our “human batteries” as much as our equipment batteries. When it’s 90 degrees outside, every unnecessary step uses energy your crew could save. Improving that workflow benefits battery runtime, the crew, and profitability.

Fall cleanups require a bigger rethink. We rely more on mowers to mulch or collect leaves instead of expecting blowers to do everything. It takes adjustment, but it can be done.

Customer expectations matter, too. The customers I’ve spoken with would rather accept a little finely mulched leaf debris than lose their peace and quiet. They want to enjoy their homes and let their kids study without constant equipment noise. We focus on the results our customers value, and their continued business tells us that approach works.

Did savings on fuel and oil costs offset the upfront cost of commercial battery banks as quickly as projected?

Based on our calculations, we save thousands of dollars annually on fuel and oil. I estimate that those savings can cover much of the initial equipment cost in about one year, or closer to two years when including a larger reserve of batteries.

Because we started with electric equipment, that’s an estimate against the cost of operating comparable gas equipment, rather than a measured before-and-after fleet conversion. The grants also made a substantial difference: combined with buying some used equipment, they covered much of our startup equipment cost and greatly reduced what we needed to pay out of pocket.

Oscar Ortega and JT Wilkinson
Maintenance Care Manager
FormLA Landscaping, Inc.

What sparked the switch to electric lawn care equipment?

Oscar: Our switch to electric equipment came more than a decade ago, as part of our philosophy of operating with optimal sustainability. We’re very proud to be the first California Air Resources Board’s first Zero Emissions Landscaper serving LA County and among the first in California.

JT: Even electric blowers are used only where it’s logical. We encourage the use of people power and logic. You won’t see a FormLA team member chasing one leaf with a blower. We sweep. We pick things up.

Did you participate in any local rebate programs when upgrading your equipment? If so, what was that experience like?

Oscar: Yes! It was really great. The California Air Resources Board (CARB) has run some great programs that work through equipment dealers. We reached out to our local ACE Hardware. Once they learned of the program, they managed much of it for us, and they also let us test equipment. They’ve become a valued part of our process.

How has working without direct gas exhaust and fuel fumes affected the daily physical health and energy levels of your crew?

JT: This is the impact we are most grateful to have made. We feel better. We hear better. We smell better — no exhaust fumes or gasoline spilled on our clothing or skin. Our team members feel better letting their kids hug them when they walk in the door. It means we are more approachable, even as we are working. It’s become an impact we mention in recruiting.

Do your clients notice a difference in your equipment choices?

Oscar: Yes, and it’s been fun to see. We didn’t promote the shift in advance, so we had clients check to see when we’d be in their gardens. We were so quiet, they didn’t notice that we’d already come and gone. Now, they brag about us and appreciate that we don’t wake babies or interrupt Zoom meetings.

What operational realities (battery rotation, charging logistics) should other contractors know if they want to reduce their fleet’s environmental footprint?

Oscar: It’s important for our teams to plug in equipment at the end of the day. We charge at night – charging shuts off automatically when the battery is full. A charge usually lasts us all day, at least in part due to our people power practices.

Did savings on fuel and oil costs offset the upfront cost of commercial battery banks as quickly as projected?

JT: We also have solar at the office, so our total cost of ownership may involve a more substantial shift. That said, even before grants and rebates were available, we almost instantaneously recouped costs.

Some of the cost savings were 100% unexpected. For example, our teams used to spend valuable time at the gas station. 20 minutes to fuel trucks, equipment, backup cans – and get snacks. Now they leave our yard ready for the day.

Advocates and Local Leaders on Making the Switch

We also spoke with advocates and local officials working to cut gas-powered leaf blower use. Ban Gas Blowers Chicago is pushing for a citywide ban in Chicago. It is part of the Quiet Clean Alliance (QCA), a national advocacy group working to eliminate gas leaf blowers. Their answers reflect an advocacy perspective.

The City of Highland Park in Lake County, Illinois (No. 30), offers a look at a different approach. In 2021, it helped form a regional working group to study gas leaf blower rules. Highland Park now limits gas blowers to operate in April, October, and November, and city staff shared how they enforce the rules, educate landscapers, and are weighing incentives.

Explore their insights below.

Ghida S. Neukirch, CM & Megan Cherry
City Manager / Management Analyst
City of Highland Park, IL

What measurable changes in community noise levels or local environmental awareness have you seen in suburbs that adopted restrictions or municipal electric fleet conversions?

Sustainability is one of the City’s core priorities, as the City has historically had a strong focus on environmental issues. The City has had regulations governing the use of gas-powered leaf blowers since the early 2000s. In an effort to reduce the noise and environmental impact associated with gas-powered leaf blowers, the City Council approved Ordinance 70-99 in 1999, which banned the use of gas-powered leaf blowers between the dates of May 15 through October 15.

This ban remained in place for several years. However, as more individuals began working from home during the COVID-19 pandemic, the City saw an increase in resident complaints pertaining to gas-powered leaf blowers, particularly as it relates to noise.

In order to address these concerns, Highland Park, along with Glencoe and Wilmette, took the lead and established the Regional Leaf Blower Working Group in 2021. The Working Group consisted of municipalities, landscapers, professional associations, environmentalists, and other professionals. The goal of the Working Group was to evaluate the need for and impact of gas-powered leaf blowers.

In 2023, based on findings of a study that the Working Group prepared, the City Council approved Ordinance O41-2023, which established the City’s current 9-month ban, where gas-powered leaf blowers are only permitted in the months of April, October, and November.

The City has issued the following citations for leaf blower violations since 2021:

  • 2021: 9 citations
  • 2022: 24 citations
  • 2023: 17 citations
  • 2024: 16 citations
  • 2025: 20 citations
  • 2026 (as of October 5): 15 citations

These numbers are a reflection of the City’s educational and enforcement efforts in order to achieve widespread compliance, positively improving residents’ quality of life in Highland Park.

How are local suburban municipalities tracking compliance or addressing opposition from landscape contractors operating across multiple townships?

In 2025, the Regional Leaf Blower Working Group entered into an agreement with the American Green Zone Alliance and Quiet Communities to conduct a study evaluating the feasibility of extending seasonal regulations on gas-powered leaf blowers. This study will provide data points that participating municipalities can utilize when considering additional regulations on gas-powered leaf blowers. This data will also be used as an educational piece when communicating these regulations to landscape contractors.

The City employs a variety of educational and enforcement measures to achieve compliance. The City’s Community Development Department primarily enforces the City’s leaf blower ordinance.

  • If inspectors witness a violation, a citation is issued without warning.
  • If the City receives a complaint, but an inspector did not witness the violation, an inspector visits the property in question and leaves an informational door hanger for the property owner that outlines the City’s ordinance. During this visit to the property, the inspector will attempt to speak to the property owner about the alleged violation and the City’s regulations.

In addition, City inspectors conduct unannounced city-wide sweeps per month, on random days, from May through September each year.

In addition to these enforcement efforts, the City educates residents and landscapers about leaf blower regulations via its various communication modalities, such as the Highlander newsletter, eNews, and social media. Educational information is shared with both residents and landscape contractors in English and Spanish.

What educational resources or incentive models have been most effective in convincing residents to voluntarily switch to electric lawn tools?

The City provides educational resources to both landscape contractors and residents. The City has primarily focused its efforts on educating and encouraging landscape contractors to use electric leaf blowers, as many Highland Park residents hire a landscape professional to perform this work. For reference, the City issued a total of 356 landscaper licenses in 2026. The City includes information about its leaf blower ordinance in its various communications to landscape contractors. Information is provided in both English and Spanish.

Although the City has not launched an informational campaign directed to residents specific to electric leaf blowers, the City’s Sustainability Advisory Group coordinates and produces the Sustainability Speaker Series on a variety of topics related to the environment, in addition to curating Sustainability Sunday posts for social media. These communications and programs are directed primarily towards residents.

However, as the City awaits the findings of the feasibility study, staff has conducted preliminary research on incentive programs offered by other communities that could be adopted by Highland Park. An incentive program, if adopted, could potentially be available to landscape contractors and/or residents in order to encourage the switch to electric leaf blowers, ensuring compliance with the City’s applicable ordinances.

Bryan D.
Co-Founder
Ban Gas Blowers Chicago

From your perspective, are municipal rebate and incentive programs in the Chicagoland area moving the needle quickly enough on commercial adoption, or do you believe mandatory policy bans are the only way to achieve meaningful emission and noise reductions?

Efforts to spur a voluntary shift, such as rebates and incentive programs, will not lead to the level of commercial adoption that legislation can achieve in the short timeframe required. Ban Gas Blowers Chicago is part of a national group called the Quiet Clean Alliance (QCA) that is working to eliminate gas leaf blowers (GLBs).

According to co-chair Judy Walton, “Cities that choose incentives and public education instead of prohibiting the use of GLBs are delaying any meaningful change. Bans are the only way to solve this out-of-control problem.” This is why Chicago suburbs have adopted legislation, and my group hopes Chicago joins them as soon as possible.

As Judy Walton pointed out, “Ending the use of gas blowers will end their assault on public health and on residents’ quality of life. It will also stop the injustice of letting low-income, largely Latino workers bear the brunt of health harms from working with GLBs for hours a day. On top of all that, it will end the damage caused by these machines to local ecosystems as well as the climate. Is it any wonder advocates are impatient for change?

How are recent gas leaf blower bans in neighboring suburbs (such as Evanston, Oak Park, and River Forest) influencing the debate at Chicago City Council, and what is your group’s current legislative strategy for citywide regulation?

We are just getting Ban Gas Blowers Chicago off the ground and hope to do more soon with regard to legislative strategy for citywide regulation. I look forward to communicating with nearby suburbs that have led the way. We encourage Chicago residents and local landscapers to reach out to us through our website and be part of the solution.

A major concern in other cities is that bans lead to flooded 311 lines or police dispatch calls for noise complaints. How do you envision fair enforcement working in a city as large as Chicago without overburdening 311 or law enforcement?

Busy 311 lines are evidence of how significant the problem is. Most residents are fed up with GLB noise and pollution.

We are learning from other cities that have had successful policies in place for several years that there are ways to design and automate the enforcement process to avoid being overburdened. And unlike enforcement of most other issues, the number of complaints diminishes significantly within a couple of years as compliance with the law increases. Ideally, enforcement becomes a non-issue over time.

It’s important to understand that enforcing a noise ordinance is far more costly and labor-intensive than enforcing a ban. With noise, an enforcement officer must rush to the site to take a sound meter reading while the violation is occurring, and if the violator doesn’t run away.

Many cities don’t have the staff or budget to enforce leaf blower decibel limits adequately. With a ban, however, residents simply submit an affidavit (sometimes with a photo), and the city follows up with the property owner through a largely administrative process until the problem is solved. For all these reasons, concerns about the enforcement burden seem to be disingenuous; just another attempt to avoid a ban.

Opponents often raise concerns about battery reliability in Midwest weather conditions and high upfront costs for commercial crews. How does your campaign address these operational challenges, and what transition support (like trade-in grants or phase-in periods) are you advocating to help local landscapers adapt?

Companies that have gone electric don’t seem to be having any issues with battery

reliability in Midwest weather conditions. We hope a few will make time to share the

knowledge they’ve gained about electric blowers with other landscapers.

The issue of higher up-front costs is often raised without mentioning the compensating lower Total Cost of Operation starting on Day One. With electric blowers, there’s no more need to buy gas (a growing expense these days) let alone oil, spark plugs, and filters. Maintenance and repair costs are also significantly less with electric tools.

Within a year or so, landscapers reach a break-even point where the extra up-front cost, if any, of purchasing an electric blower has been recouped, and then it’s pure savings for the landscaper compared to having a gas blower. And when making larger profits, there should be no need to raise fees.

While we don’t think transition support is always necessary, we’ll certainly consider an appropriate phase-in schedule or funding to help micro-businesses with up-front costs. But the beauty of a ban is that it sets a level playing field for all landscapers. That should be the extent of the government’s role.

After 30+ years, the evidence in support of banning these machines is overwhelming. You can read some of the best articles and reports on QCA’s site.

Ranking and Methodology

We compared 652 U.S. counties with populations above 50,000 across 15 metrics.

Our metrics covered 4 main themes:

  • Lawn Equipment Pollution Rank (~42%): Tons of PM 2.5 (2023), CO2 (2020), NOx (2023), VOC (2023), and CO (2023) emissions from gas-powered lawn equipment. 
  • Mowing Intensity Rank (~29%): Total residential yard area (2024), golf courses per 100,000 residents (2026), share of single-unit detached homes (2024), and acres of developed open space (2024). 
  • Air Quality Burden Rank (~17%): Median AQI (2025), PM 2.5 concentration (2020), number of unhealthy AQI days (2025), and the annual mean of the daily 8-hour average ozone concentration (2022). 
  • Community & Economic Context Rank (~12%): The number of landscaping businesses per 100,000 residents (2023 and 2026 data) and population density (2024). 

For each of the 652 counties with available data and populations above 50,000, we then gathered the most recent data available on each metric from the sources listed below. 

Finally, we calculated scores (out of 100 points) for each county to determine its rank in each metric, each category, and overall. A county’s Overall Score is the weighted average of its scores across all metrics and categories. The highest Overall Score ranked “Highest Potential Impact” (No. 1) and the lowest “Lowest Potential Impact” (No. 652).

Notes:

  • The lowest rank among individual factors may not be No. 652 due to ties. 
  • Lawn Equipment Pollution metrics only include mowers/tractors/turf equipment and leaf blowers/trimmers/edgers across gas/diesel/LPG variants. They exclude chainsaws and snowblowers.
  • Car conversion data are calculated using EPA’s figure that a typical passenger vehicle emits 4.6 metric tons of CO2 per year. 
  • To estimate total residential lawn area, we multiplied average yard size by the number of single-unit detached homes.
  • To calculate the developed open space, we counted pixels from the National Land Cover Database of "Developed, Open Space" — residential lawns, parks, golf courses, cemeteries, and low-impervious developed land.
  • Unhealthy AQI days include the number of days in 2025 that were recorded as Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups Days, Unhealthy Days, Very Unhealthy Days, and Hazardous Days by the EPA. 

Sources: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, County Health Rankings & Roadmaps, U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, U.S. Census Bureau, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, U.S. Federal Housing Finance Agency, U.S. Geological Survey, and Open Street Map

Better for the Environment, and Better for You

Reducing pollution isn’t the only reason for switching to electric lawn equipment. 

Noise Reduction

For Kevin Boodram of Serenity Robotic Lawncare, “Noise was the biggest motivation. I was in school during the pandemic, and gas leaf blowers kept waking me up and interrupting my remote classes.”

Boodram’s customers noticed a difference: “One customer described us as ‘ninjas.’ They would go into a meeting with an overgrown lawn, come out to find it cut, and never realize we had been there,” he says.

“We didn’t promote the shift in advance, so we had clients check to see when we’d be in their gardens,” says Oscar Ortega of FormLA Landscaping, Inc. “We were so quiet, they didn’t notice that we’d already come and gone. Now, they brag about us, and appreciate that we don’t wake babies or interrupt Zoom meetings.”

Saving Fuel (and Time)

“Even before grants and rebates were available, we almost instantaneously recouped costs,” says JT Wilkinson of FormLA Landscaping, Inc. “Some of the cost savings were 100% unexpected. For example, our teams used to spend valuable time at the gas station: 20 minutes to fuel trucks, equipment, backup cans, and get snacks. Now they leave our yard ready for the day.”

Ban Gas Blowers Chicago makes a similar case: “With electric blowers there’s no more
need to buy gas (a growing expense these days), let alone oil, spark plugs, and filters.
Maintenance and repair costs are also significantly less with electric tools. Within a year or so, landscapers reach a break-even point where the extra up-front cost, if any, of purchasing an electric blower has been recouped, and then it’s pure savings for the landscaper compared to having a gas blower,” says Bryan D.

Health Benefits

“In my experience, electric equipment makes the workday much less physically taxing,” Boodram says.

Wilkinson agrees: “We feel better. We hear better. We smell better. No exhaust fumes or gasoline spilled on our clothing or skin. Our team members feel better letting their kids hug them when they walk in the door. It means we are more approachable, even as we are working. It’s become an impact we mention in recruiting.”
